subject: piti is not your expenses
preheader: the 50 percent rule and where it actually breaks.
headline: PITI covers four things. Operating a rental needs about nine.
body: PITI is principal, interest, taxes, insurance. That's the mortgage payment. New investors often plug PITI into a deal, subtract from rent, and call the rest 'cash flow.' It isn't.

Real operating expenses also include: property management, vacancy, repairs and maintenance, CapEx reserves, lawn/snow if applicable, utilities you pay (often water/sewer in multifamily), turnover costs, and the random stuff (pest, HOA, etc).

The 50% rule says: assume operating expenses (everything except debt service) will equal 50% of gross rent over the long run. So a $2,000/mo rental nets about $1,000/mo before mortgage. Whatever's left after PITI is your real cash flow.

Where it breaks: brand new construction (closer to 35-40%), Class C properties in tough markets (often 55-60%), and high-tax states like NJ or TX (sometimes 55%+ just from property tax). The 50% rule is a sanity check, not a substitute for line-item underwriting.
TrueCap line-items every expense category by default and pre-fills tax and insurance estimates. You can see the full operating expense number before you decide whether to dig deeper.
